title: Split back stitch
subtitle: Back stitch worked by piercing the previous stitch for a tighter chain
excerpt: Split back stitch works like back stitch but the emerging needle pierces the thread of the previous stitch rather than emerging beside it. The result is a tighter, more chain-like line that hugs curves precisely.
sourceNotes: Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882), split back stitch entry. Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), outline variations chapter (Project Gutenberg #20776).

glossaryTerms.definition: The interlocked appearance produced when each stitch pierces the thread of the last, rather than emerging cleanly beside it.

heroPrompt: Split back stitch in burgundy stranded cotton on pale linen, a tight curved outline showing the chain-like joins, close view, daylight.

content.text: outline by combining the backwards motion of back stitch with the piercing action of split stitch. Every stitch goes back to meet the previous one and splits through it, locking them together.
Bring the thread up at A and take a forward stitch to B. Pull through.
Bring the needle up at the midpoint of the AB stitch, piercing the thread strands.
Insert backwards to B (sharing the stitch hole), emerge at the midpoint of this new stitch.
Continue: each stitch goes backward to the previous hole and splits through the previous stitch on emergence.

attrs.heading: When split back stitch goes wrong

items.symptom: The outline looks like plain back stitch, no chain effect
items.cause: Needle is emerging beside the previous stitch rather than through it.
items.fix: The emerging needle must physically pierce the thread bundle. Work slowly until the piercing action is reliable.
Mark stitch-length intervals on the transfer line with small dots before starting.

content.text: Split back stitch is preferred for very fine curved outlines where split stitch alone is not tight enough. It is used in whitework and goldwork for precise border lines.
